newsitem.title: CONGO: Mortar bombs blast Congo's battered Brazzaville.
newsitem.headline: Mortar bombs blast Congo's battered Brazzaville.

text.p: Fresh fighting erupted in the Congolese capital of Brazzaville on Wednesday, with mortar bombs slamming into the city centre and a landmark hotel by the Congo river.
The bombs fell around the French embassy in the central area, controlled by the forces of President Pascal Lissouba.
The firing appeared to come from the north, held by his rival, former military leader Denis Sassou Nguesso.
One bomb crashed into the 11-storey Sofitel hotel, one of few high-rise buildings in the city of a million people.
A charter airline pilot due to fly into Brazzaville on Wednesday cancelled the flight, saying it seemed that Sassou's forces were battling to gain control of the airport.
French ambassador Raymond Cesaire had to abandon a trip to meet the plane because of shooting near the airport, a prime target for the warring parties.
A shaky week-old ceasefire has dampened but failed to stop clashes between Lissouba and Sassou, whose 12 days of battles erupted on June 5 and have left 1,000 to 3,000 people dead.
The United Nations is trying to recruit peacekeepers to separate the two sides, whose front line cuts through the heart of the city, but says a proper truce is a precondition.
U.N. envoy Mohamed Sahnoun has said the force's first task will be to take control of the airport, which French forces abandoned last Friday after evacuating thousands of foreigners.
Sahnoun also said that the Congolese had to earn the force by showing the will to find a political reconciliation.
"It's on this point that things are jammed, it is very difficult," Cesaire, the only foreign envoy left in Brazzaville, said before the fighting resumed.
"It needs time. Let's cross our fingers."
Togo and Senegal have offered troops for the mission of an expected 1,700 soldiers.
Cesaire, protected by 30 gendarmes, has been shuttling between Lissouba, Sassou and city mayor Bernard Kolelas, who heads a National Mediation Committee.
France's 12 diplomats and the gendarmes are among a handful of foreigners left in Brazzaville that also includes some missionaries and international Red Cross workers.

Many of the city's diplomats and expatriate businessfolk have decamped to Pointe Noire, Congo's Atlantic Ocean port which, like the rest of the oil-producing country, has been untouched by the fighting in the capital.
Mediation efforts are aimed at getting residential elections, due on July 27 but postponed due to the fighting, back on track.
Lissouba is trying to get a constitutional council to extend his term of office until October because of the chaos. Sassou says Lissouba is no longer fit to rule and must step down now.
